newsitem.title: JAPAN: US Treasuries 10-yr note, long bond up in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries 10-yr note, long bond up in Tokyo.

text.p: The U.S. Treasuries 10-year note and the key long bond rose in response to bids by bargain hunters in thin Tokyo trading on Tuesday.
The 6-5/8 percent 10-year note was last traded at 99-8/32 or a yield of 6.73 percent at 0157 GMT, up from Friday's New York close of 99-4/32.
The benchmark 6-5/8 percent 30-year long bond was last quoted at 95-20/32 or a yield of 6.97 percent, compared with New York's 95-15/32.
Most Japanese institutional investors appeared content to stay on the sidelines, traders said.

The market focus is on whether U.S. hedge funds, which were estimated to have unloaded several billion dollars worth of Treasuries last week, will keep dumping notes and bonds in the post holiday market, traders said.

Those sales by the funds partly reflected the unwinding of the so-called "yen-carry trade" in which they borrowed low-cost yen funds and changed them into dollars for U.S. Treasuries and equities investment, traders said.
However, recent rises in yen interest rates, along with the yen's steep appreciation, have forced the funds to pay back yen funds by cashing in the Treasuries, they added.
Other traders said the funds' sales in Treasuries also reflected their attempt to make up heavy losses they have recently incurred by speculation in the Thai baht.

The baht/dollar forex market has been divided into offshore and local markets since the Bank of Thailand's move in mid-May to cut off offshore players' access to the baht to fend off speculators' attacks.

"Hedge funds may have needed to generate cash (by selling off Treasuries ) as they have suffered significant losses on their long baht positions which were further worsened by an inability to liquidate positions," said a brokerage trader.

"They (the U.S. funds), as many others, have overestimated emerging market economies, while underestimating Tokyo and assuming that yen interest rates would remain trifling due to (Japan's) banking sector woes," said the brokerage trader.
Some said the U.S. hedge funds selling of Treasuries also mirrored attempts to unwind their positions by selling short-term debt and buying long-term debt.
Those funds are still holding long positions in Treasuries and their activities will set the market tone on Tuesday, they said.
